hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: An ad click aggregator must report clicks per ad for each non-overlapping 1-minute bucket (12:00-12:01, 12:01-12:02, ...). Which window type fits?
options: Sliding window of 1 minute that advances every 10 seconds
Tumbling window of 1 minute
Session window with a 1-minute inactivity gap
A single global window triggered every minute
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Tumbling windows are fixed-size and non-overlapping, so each click lands in exactly one minute bucket. A sliding/hopping window overlaps, so one click would be counted in several windows.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: Mobile clients buffer clicks offline and deliver them up to 3 minutes late. Billing must attribute each click to the minute it actually happened. What should the aggregation job use?
options: Processing-time windows, since late data averages out over a day
Windows keyed on the time the event reached the stream processor
Event-time windows with a watermark that tolerates about 3 minutes of lateness
Hold every window open indefinitely until no more data can arrive
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Event-time windows assign clicks by when they occurred; a watermark with allowed lateness lets windows close once late data is unlikely. Processing-time windows would put late clicks into the wrong minute, which matters for billing.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: In a stream processor such as Apache Flink, what does a watermark with timestamp 12:05:00 assert?
options: All events up to wall-clock time 12:05:00 on the worker have been processed
The consumer has committed Kafka offsets for everything produced before 12:05:00
A checkpoint containing state as of 12:05:00 has completed
No more events with event time earlier than 12:05:00 are expected, so windows ending by then may fire
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: A watermark is a (heuristic) statement about event-time progress: events older than it are not expected, so windows ending at or before it can emit. It is unrelated to wall-clock time, offsets or checkpoints.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: A Flink job reads clicks from Kafka, computes per-minute counts, and inserts rows into a SQL table. After a crash and restore from the last checkpoint, some minutes appear twice in the table. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The sink is not idempotent or transactional; upsert keyed by (ad_id, window_start) or use a two-phase-commit sink
The checkpoint interval is too short; increase it so fewer checkpoints are replayed
Kafka auto-commit was disabled; enable it so offsets are committed on every poll
Event time was used; switch to processing time so replayed events fall into new windows
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Restoring from a checkpoint replays input since that checkpoint, so windows can be emitted again. Exactly-once end to end needs an idempotent (upsert) or transactional sink. Enabling Kafka auto-commit would bypass Flink's checkpointed offsets and can lose data.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: What is the main operational criticism of the Lambda architecture that the Kappa architecture addresses?
options: Lambda cannot serve low-latency queries because everything goes through batch jobs
The same business logic has to be built and kept consistent in two separate systems, a batch layer and a speed layer
Lambda cannot store raw events, so historical recomputation is impossible
Lambda requires exactly-once delivery from the message broker to work at all
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Lambda runs a batch layer and a speed layer whose outputs are merged, so the same logic lives in two codebases that must agree. Kappa uses one streaming pipeline and reprocesses by replaying the log. Lambda does serve low latency through its speed layer.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: In a Kappa architecture you fix a bug in the click-aggregation logic and need to recompute the last 30 days. How is this normally done?
options: Run a nightly batch job over a data warehouse copy and merge it with the stream output
Edit the aggregate rows in place with SQL updates that apply the correction
Restore the job from its latest checkpoint so recent windows are recomputed
Start the fixed job as a new consumer from the start of the retained log, write to a new table, and switch readers once it catches up
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Kappa reprocessing replays the immutable log (which must retain at least 30 days) through the corrected job into a fresh output, then cuts over. Restoring the latest checkpoint only replays a few minutes and would keep the old bug for older windows.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: A viral ad sends 40% of all clicks to one ad_id, overloading the single task that owns that key. Which mitigation works best?
options: Add more Kafka partitions so the hot key spreads across more consumers
Increase the window size so the hot key emits fewer results
Salt the key into N sub-keys (ad_id#0..N-1), pre-aggregate in parallel, then merge the partial counts in a second stage
Switch the job from event time to processing time to reduce buffering
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Salting spreads one hot key across many tasks and a second stage combines partial sums, which works because counts are associative. More partitions don't help: one key still hashes to one partition and one task.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: Which statements about session windows are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Their length is determined by gaps in activity rather than a fixed size
Two sessions for the same key can merge when a late event fills the gap between them
Their start and end times are known as soon as the first event arrives
They suit analytics like 'clicks per user visit'
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Session windows close after an inactivity gap, so their bounds depend on the data and can merge when a late event bridges two sessions. Because they are data-driven, the end time is not known when the first event arrives.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: An ad click aggregator must produce accurate billing counts and a real-time dashboard. Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Deduplicate clicks by click_id within a bounded time window before counting
Periodically reconcile streaming results against a batch recomputation over stored raw events
Use processing-time windows for billing because they are simpler to operate
Keep raw click events in durable storage such as object storage for audits and recomputation
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Dedup, reconciliation and keeping raw events are standard for money-related counts. Processing-time windows attribute late clicks to the wrong period, which is unacceptable for billing even if fine for a rough dashboard.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: A hopping (sliding) window of size 10 minutes that advances every 1 minute assigns each event to 10 windows.
options: True
False
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Each event belongs to size / slide = 10 / 1 = 10 overlapping windows. This is why sliding windows cost more state and output than tumbling windows of the same size.

hld-analytics-scheduler:0.prompt: In a Kappa architecture, reprocessing historical data is impossible, so a separate batch layer is still required.
options: True
False
hld-analytics-scheduler:0.explanation: Kappa reprocesses by replaying the retained log through a new version of the streaming job. The batch layer is exactly what Kappa removes; the requirement is long enough log retention (or tiered storage).

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: In Redis, which command adds 50 points to player:42 in the sorted set 'leaderboard', creating the member if it doesn't exist?
options: INCRBY leaderboard:player:42 50
HINCRBY leaderboard player:42 50
ZADD leaderboard NX 50 player:42
ZINCRBY leaderboard 50 player:42
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: ZINCRBY increments a member's score in a sorted set and creates it if missing. ZADD with NX only adds new members and never updates existing scores, so it would ignore the increment for returning players.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: What is the time complexity of ZINCRBY on a Redis sorted set with N members?
options: O(log N)
O(N)
O(N log N)
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: Sorted sets use a skip list plus a hash table, so updating a score and repositioning the member is O(log N). The O(1) hash lookup finds the member, but the reorder in the skip list is logarithmic.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: Scores are 'higher is better'. Which Redis command returns player:42's 0-based rank where rank 0 is the top scorer?
options: ZRANK leaderboard player:42
ZREVRANK leaderboard player:42
ZSCORE leaderboard player:42
ZCOUNT leaderboard player:42 +inf
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: ZREVRANK ranks from highest to lowest score. ZRANK ranks ascending, so it would give 0 to the lowest scorer; ZSCORE returns the score, not the rank.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: Which command returns the top 10 players with their scores, highest first (Redis 6.2+)?
options: ZRANGE leaderboard 0 10 WITHSCORES
ZRANGEBYSCORE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES
ZRANGE leaderboard 0 9 REV WITHSCORES
ZREVRANK leaderboard 0 9
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: ZRANGE with REV and index range 0..9 returns the 10 highest-scored members (ZREVRANGE does the same in older versions). '0 10' is inclusive and returns 11 members in ascending order; ZRANGEBYSCORE 0 9 filters by score values, not positions.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: Two players have equal scores, and the one who reached the score first should rank higher. How do you implement this with a Redis sorted set?
options: Nothing extra: Redis breaks ties by insertion time automatically
Encode a tiebreaker into the score, e.g. points * 10^10 + (MAX_TS - achievedAtSeconds), keeping values within 2^53
Use ZADD GT so the earlier score cannot be overwritten
Store timestamps in a separate hash; ZRANGE reads it when scores are equal
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: Redis orders equal scores lexicographically by member name, not by time, so the tiebreak must be folded into the score. Scores are doubles, so the composite must stay below 2^53 to remain exact.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: A Count-Min Sketch counts search-query frequencies with only non-negative increments. What kind of error can its estimates have?
options: Only underestimates, because collisions cancel out
Errors in both directions, symmetric around the true count
Exact counts for frequent items and zero for rare ones
Only overestimates, because hash collisions add other items' counts
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: Each counter cell collects the counts of every item hashing to it, and the estimate is the minimum over rows, so it can only be equal to or above the true count. It never underestimates with non-negative updates.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: A leaderboard is sharded across 8 Redis nodes by user id (one sorted set per shard). How do you get the exact global top 100?
options: Fetch the top 100 from every shard and merge the 800 candidates, keeping the best 100
Fetch the top 13 from each shard (100/8, rounded up) and merge them
Run ZUNIONSTORE across the 8 keys on the cluster and read the result
Write every score to one key and read from its replicas to spread load
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: Any user in the global top 100 must be in the top 100 of their own shard, so the union of per-shard top-100s contains the answer. Taking 13 per shard fails if one shard holds most top players; ZUNIONSTORE fails across hash slots in Redis Cluster.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: Which are valid techniques for finding approximate top-K heavy hitters in a very high-volume stream with bounded memory? Select all that apply.
options: A Count-Min Sketch combined with a min-heap of the current K best items
The Space-Saving (or Misra-Gries) algorithm with a fixed number of counters
A HyperLogLog per item to estimate how often each item occurs
A Bloom filter that reports how many times each item was inserted
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: CMS plus a heap and Space-Saving/Misra-Gries are classic bounded-memory frequency algorithms. HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements, not frequencies, and a Bloom filter only answers membership.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: Which statements about Redis sorted sets are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Members are unique; adding an existing member updates its score
Scores are double-precision floats, so integers above 2^53 can lose precision
ZRANGEBYSCORE costs O(log N + M), where M is the number of returned elements
They are backed only by a hash table, so every range query scans all members
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: Sorted sets combine a hash table (member to score) with a skip list ordered by score, which is why range queries are O(log N + M). Scores are IEEE-754 doubles, so very large integers are not exact.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: Running ZINCRBY for a member that is not yet in the sorted set creates it with the increment as its score.
options: True
False
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: ZINCRBY treats a missing member as having score 0, so it is created with the increment. That makes it safe for the first score event of a new player.

hld-analytics-scheduler:1.prompt: When any item can appear on any server, merging each server's local top-K list always yields the exact global top-K.
options: True
False
hld-analytics-scheduler:1.explanation: An item ranked K+1 on every server never appears in any local list, yet its combined count could be the global #1. Merging local top-K lists is only exact when each item's full count lives on a single server, for example when partitioned by item key.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: A Node service schedules a daily email job with node-cron and runs on 3 replicas. Users get the email three times. What is the right fix?
options: Add random jitter to the cron start time on each replica
Configure each replica to run the job at a different minute
Make sure only one executor runs each scheduled run, e.g. via a lease in a shared store or a single scheduler service
Increase the job's retry count so failed replicas stop retrying
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: Every replica runs its own in-process cron, so the job fires once per replica. You need coordination (a lease or a dedicated scheduler) so one run is claimed by one worker. Jitter or staggered minutes still runs it three times.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: Why should a worker's claim on a scheduled job be a lease with an expiry rather than a lock with no TTL?
options: If the worker crashes, the claim expires and another worker can take the job
Leases are faster to acquire than locks in every database
Locks without TTL cannot be shared across machines
Leases guarantee that each job runs exactly once
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: A crashed holder never releases a TTL-less lock, so the job is stuck forever. A lease frees itself after expiry. It does not guarantee exactly-once: a slow holder may still be running when the lease passes to someone else.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: Worker A holds a job lease, then hits a 40-second GC pause. The lease expires, worker B takes it and writes results. A wakes up and writes stale results. What prevents A's write?
options: Use a longer lease TTL so pauses never exceed it
Have A check that it still holds the lease right before writing
Acquire the lease with Redis SET NX instead of a database row
Issue a monotonically increasing fencing token with each lease and have storage reject writes with an older token
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: With fencing tokens, the storage itself refuses writes from an older lease holder, which closes the race. Checking the lease before writing still leaves a gap between the check and the write in which A can pause again.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: In PostgreSQL, several workers poll a jobs table for due jobs. Which approach lets them claim different rows concurrently without blocking each other?
options: SELECT due rows, then UPDATE them to 'running' without any row lock
SELECT ... FOR SHARE on the due rows, then mark them 'running'
SELECT ... ORDER BY run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a transaction, then mark them 'running'
LOCK TABLE jobs IN EXCLUSIVE MODE before every poll
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED locks the selected rows and makes other workers skip them instead of waiting, so each worker gets a different batch. FOR SHARE lets several workers lock the same row, so two of them can claim it.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: A scheduled job calls a flaky third-party API. Which retry policy is most appropriate?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds
Exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum attempt count, then a dead-letter queue
Retry every second forever with a fixed delay
Never retry; let the next scheduled run pick up the work
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: Backoff with jitter avoids hammering a struggling dependency and prevents synchronized retry storms; a cap plus a DLQ keeps permanent failures visible. Tight loops or fixed infinite retries amplify outages.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: A scheduler was down for 6 hours. An hourly job that rolls up billing for 'the previous hour' missed 6 runs. What should happen on recovery?
options: Run once now, covering only the most recent hour
Skip the missed runs; the next scheduled run will catch up
Fire the job 6 times concurrently with no identifiers
Create one run per missed scheduled time, keyed by (job_id, scheduled_for), so each hour is processed once
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: Each hourly window must be processed, and keying runs by their scheduled time makes the backfill idempotent if recovery itself is retried. Running once covers only one hour; untracked concurrent runs can't be deduplicated.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: Why must scheduled jobs be idempotent even when you use leases?
options: Cron expressions can trigger twice within the same minute
Execution is effectively at-least-once: a crash or lease expiry can re-run a job that partly or fully completed
Idempotent jobs run faster because the database caches them
Leases require idempotent jobs to be stored in a queue
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: A worker can finish the side effect and crash before marking the run done; the lease expires and another worker repeats it. Idempotency (unique keys, upserts) makes that repeat harmless. Cron itself fires once per matching minute.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: You are designing a distributed job scheduler. Which practices are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Store job definitions and next_run_at durably, with an index on next_run_at for polling
Have long-running workers heartbeat to extend their leases
Keep the schedule only in the leader's memory to avoid database load
Compute next_run_at with explicit time zones so DST changes are handled deliberately
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: Durable, indexed schedules, lease heartbeats and explicit time-zone handling are standard. A schedule held only in the leader's memory is lost when the leader fails, which defeats the point of a distributed scheduler.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: Jobs are scheduled in local time in America/New_York. Which DST-related statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A job at 02:30 local time may be skipped on the spring-forward day because that time does not exist
A job at 01:30 local time may run twice on the fall-back day because that hour repeats
A job scheduled at 12:00 UTC shifts by an hour in UTC terms when DST starts
Scheduling in UTC avoids gaps and repeats, but the job's local wall-clock time moves by an hour across seasons
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: In the US, clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00 in spring (02:30 doesn't exist) and from 02:00 back to 01:00 in autumn (01:00-01:59 happens twice). UTC has no DST, so a UTC schedule never shifts in UTC; it only shifts relative to local time.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: A Redis lock taken with SET key value NX PX 30000 guarantees mutual exclusion even if the holder pauses for longer than 30 seconds.
options: True
False
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: After 30 seconds the key expires and another client can acquire it while the paused holder still believes it owns the lock. Safety then needs fencing tokens or idempotent side effects.

hld-analytics-scheduler:2.prompt: With visibility timeouts (as in Amazon SQS), a message whose processing takes longer than the timeout can be delivered to another consumer while the first is still working on it.
options: True
False
hld-analytics-scheduler:2.explanation: When the visibility timeout expires without a delete, the message becomes visible again and can be received by another consumer. Long jobs should extend the timeout (ChangeMessageVisibility) and be idempotent.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: Which statement describes Prometheus's default collection model?
options: Agents push metrics to the server over UDP
Services write samples directly into the server's TSDB files
The server scrapes HTTP /metrics endpoints of discovered targets at a fixed interval
The server tails application log files and parses metrics from them
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: Prometheus pulls: it discovers targets and scrapes their /metrics endpoints on an interval. Push-style UDP ingestion is the StatsD model, not Prometheus's default.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: A batch job runs for 20 seconds and Prometheus scrapes every 30 seconds. The job's metrics rarely show up. What is the standard fix?
options: Push the job's final metrics to a Pushgateway (or an OTLP collector) before it exits
Lower the scrape interval to 1 second for all targets
Increase Prometheus retention so the samples are kept longer
Use counters instead of gauges so values accumulate
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: A pull model can't scrape a process that is gone. Short-lived jobs push to an intermediary that Prometheus then scrapes. A 1-second interval across all targets multiplies load and still races the job's exit.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: What is a genuine advantage of the pull model over push for metrics collection?
options: It works more easily for targets behind NAT or firewalls
It needs no service discovery because targets announce themselves
It gives lower latency for very short-lived processes
A failed scrape tells the server the target is down, and the server controls its own ingestion rate
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: With pull, a failed scrape sets up=0, giving built-in health detection, and the server decides how much it ingests. Working behind NAT is a push advantage, and pull does require service discovery.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: A team adds a user_id label to http_requests_total and Prometheus memory usage explodes. Why?
options: Labels are stored as strings inside each sample, making every sample larger
Every unique label combination is a separate time series, and user_id makes the series count huge
Adding labels doubles the scrape frequency for that metric
Counters with labels force histogram buckets to be recomputed
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: Series count is the product of label value counts; millions of user ids create millions of series, each with its own in-memory index and chunk. Unbounded values like user ids belong in logs or traces, not metric labels.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: Why do time-series databases such as Facebook's Gorilla and Prometheus compress samples so well (often around 1-2 bytes per sample)?
options: Each sample is gzipped individually before being written
Only changed values are stored, indexed in a B-tree
Regular timestamps give near-zero delta-of-deltas, and similar consecutive values XOR to few significant bits
Duplicate samples are hashed and removed across all series
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: Delta-of-delta encoding turns evenly spaced timestamps into mostly zeros, and XOR-ing consecutive floats leaves few meaningful bits when values change slowly. Per-sample gzip would add overhead rather than remove it.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: You downsample raw 10-second p99 latency into 5-minute points by averaging the p99 values. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong, but it loses the original timestamps
Percentiles cannot be correctly averaged or re-aggregated; keep histogram bucket counts or sketches and compute p99 from the merged distribution
You should take the max of the p99 values, which gives the exact 5-minute p99
Downsampling must always use the median instead of the mean
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: The p99 of a combined period is not the mean of sub-period p99s, especially with uneven traffic. Mergeable structures (histograms, t-digest, DDSketch) allow correct percentiles after rollup. The max of p99s is an upper bound, not the exact value.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: A metrics platform keeps raw data for 15 days, 5-minute rollups for 90 days and 1-hour rollups for 2 years. What is the main reason?
options: Cut storage and long-range query cost while keeping full detail for recent data
Rollups make old data more accurate than the raw samples
Counters can only be stored after being rolled up
It speeds up writes, since raw samples are rejected after 15 days
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: Most queries over months only need coarse resolution, so rollups shrink storage and make dashboards spanning a year fast. Rollups lose detail; they never make data more accurate.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: Which per-bucket rollups can be correctly combined into coarser buckets later? Select all that apply.
options: Sum and count (so the average can be derived)
Minimum and maximum
The plain mean of bucket averages when buckets have different sample counts
The 95th percentile of each bucket's 95th percentile
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: Sum, count, min and max are mergeable: combining them gives the exact value for the larger bucket. An unweighted mean of averages is biased when sample counts differ, and percentiles of percentiles are not the true percentile.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: Which statements about Prometheus counters and rate() are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Counters only go up, except when they reset to zero, e.g. on process restart
rate() detects counter resets and compensates for them
Apply sum() before rate(), i.e. rate(sum(x)), to get correct totals across instances
rate() needs at least two samples in the range window to return a value
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: rate() handles resets per series and needs two or more samples. You must rate first and then sum, sum(rate(x[5m])), because summing raw counters hides the individual resets and produces bogus spikes.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: In a pure push model, the monitoring backend cannot easily distinguish a dead service from one that simply has nothing to report.
options: True
False
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: Missing pushes are ambiguous: the service may be down, partitioned or idle. Push setups add heartbeats or absence alerts; pull gets a failed scrape as an explicit signal.

hld-analytics-scheduler:3.prompt: Time-series databases are typically optimized for frequent random in-place updates of historical data points.
options: True
False
hld-analytics-scheduler:3.explanation: TSDBs are optimized for append-mostly writes of recent data and range reads over time, storing samples in immutable compressed blocks. Rewriting old points is rare and expensive.
